speaker: Tim Latimer
title: Tim Latimer on Solving the Financing Problem for Geothermal
question: For emerging clean-power technologies, why do large corporate buyers typically sign the first commercial offtake agreements before electric utilities will?
guest: Our first offtake agreement was with Google in 2021, and it wasn't an accident that it was Google. They put out a white paper in 2018 saying they'd achieved their 100% renewable energy goal—which is really an annual accounting exercise—and introduced a stricter standard of 24/7 carbon-free energy, which is hourly matching where and when facilities actually use power. Their point was that wind and solar have been phenomenal, but we need a new toolkit like geothermal to get there. It took a company like Google because utilities want to see a track record, and I don't fault them for it. They're responsible for keeping the lights on, so if they invest the time to prepare the grid, the resource needs to show up. Most utilities won't even look at something until it has a multi-year operating track record, creating a chicken-and-egg problem. Not everybody has geologists sitting around, but a company like Google had the resources and technical expertise to work with us over a multi-year period, learn how our technology worked, and unlock that first operation.

points.core: Electric utilities require multi-year operating track records because they guarantee grid reliability.
points.note: Accept: utilities are accountable for keeping the lights on and cannot risk grid-planning investments on unproven generation. Do not credit: generic claims that utilities are slow or bureaucratic without tying it to reliability responsibility.

points.core: Hourly carbon-free energy targets expose gaps that intermittent renewables alone cannot cover.
points.note: Accept: moving from annual 100% renewable accounting to 24/7 hourly matching creates corporate demand for firm clean baseload power. Do not credit: generic statements that tech companies care about ESG or sustainability.

points.core: Large corporate buyers have dedicated technical teams capable of evaluating unproven energy technologies.
points.note: Accept: hyperscalers possess the financial resources and internal engineering expertise to partner over multiple years on first-of-a-kind projects. Do not credit: saying only that tech companies have more money without noting technical underwriting capacity.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
It comes down to who can bear first-of-a-kind risk and pay a premium for it.

Regulated utilities are structurally conservative. Their spending must pass "prudency" review by state regulators, who require least-cost procurement on behalf of captive ratepayers. An unproven technology with a high first-of-a-kind price, uncertain construction schedule and performance risk is hard to justify, and if the project overruns or fails, regulators may disallow cost recovery, leaving shareholders with the loss. Utilities also have a legal obligation to deliver reliable service, so they favour proven assets, and their approval processes are slow.

Large corporate buyers, especially technology companies, face none of those constraints. They have large balance sheets and strong credit, can voluntarily pay a "green premium," and answer to shareholders rather than rate regulators. They also have strong motives: rapidly growing data-centre load, ambitious 24/7 carbon-free commitments, and a strategic interest in driving technologies down the cost curve.

Their creditworthy long-term contracts make early projects financeable, as seen with Google–Fervo (enhanced geothermal), Google–Kairos and Amazon–X-energy (advanced nuclear), and Microsoft–Helion (fusion). Utilities typically follow once cost and performance are demonstrated.

points.why: The response directly ties utilities’ preference for demonstrated performance to their obligation to deliver reliable service.
quotes: Utilities also have a legal obligation to deliver reliable service, so they favour proven assets
Utilities typically follow once cost and performance are demonstrated.

points.why: The response mentions 24/7 carbon-free commitments without explaining how hourly matching exposes gaps in wind and solar output and creates demand for firm clean power.
The response describes corporate financial capacity but omits the in-house technical expertise needed to evaluate unproven technologies.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Electric utilities operate under strict regulatory mandates designed to protect captive ratepayers, requiring public utility commissions to approve power purchases under "least-cost" and "prudence" standards. First-of-a-kind clean technologies—such as advanced geothermal, next-generation nuclear, and long-duration storage—carry steep cost premiums, unproven performance, and schedule risks. Regulators rarely allow utilities to pass those risks onto customers, and utilities avoid risking cost disallowances on their own balance sheets. Slow, rigid integrated resource planning and competitive bidding cycles further bias utilities toward mature, bankable generation, while their statutory duty to maintain grid reliability leaves little tolerance for project delays or underperformance.

Large corporate buyers, particularly cash-rich technology firms, answer to shareholders rather than rate regulators, giving them freedom to absorb early commercial risks. Driven by surging data-center power demand and ambitious round-the-clock decarbonization targets, corporates willingly pay green premiums and tolerate development delays to secure scarce firm clean capacity and catalyze learning-curve cost reductions. Able to negotiate flexible bilateral contracts rapidly, they de-risk emerging technologies until costs and reliability satisfy utility regulators.

points.why: The response links utilities’ preference for proven generation to their responsibility for grid reliability.
quotes: bias utilities toward mature, bankable generation
their statutory duty to maintain grid reliability leaves little tolerance for project delays or underperformance

points.why: The response links round-the-clock goals to demand for firm clean power but leaves out the gaps that intermittent renewables create under hourly matching.
The response describes financial flexibility and contracting speed without identifying the in-house technical expertise needed to evaluate unproven technologies.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Large corporate buyers usually sign first because they can pay for new technology in ways utilities are not allowed to. Most utilities are rate-regulated. Commissions generally expect them to buy the least-cost, proven resources that keep the grid reliable, and if a contract later looks imprudent, regulators can refuse to let them recover the cost from customers. A first-of-a-kind geothermal, advanced nuclear or long-duration storage project costs more and carries technology and schedule risk that is hard to justify in a rate case. Utility planning and procurement cycles also run for years.

Companies like Google, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta face different incentives. They have voluntary climate goals, some aiming for 24/7 carbon-free power. They also need firm power for fast-growing data centers, have strong balance sheets, and can treat a price premium as a small strategic cost. Being early gains them supply access, influence over project design and public credibility. Their contracts give lenders bankable revenue to finance early plants, such as Google's deals with Fervo and Kairos or Microsoft's with Helion. Those early plants help bring costs down until utilities and regulators see the technology as prudent enough to buy at scale.

points.why: The response ties utilities’ preference for proven resources to their responsibility for grid reliability.
quotes: Commissions generally expect them to buy the least-cost, proven resources that keep the grid reliable

points.why: The response mentions 24/7 targets and firm power without explaining how hourly matching exposes gaps in wind and solar generation.
The response describes buyers’ financial capacity and influence over project design but gives no evidence of in-house expertise to evaluate unproven technologies.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Regulated electric utilities operate under strict public-interest mandates that require them to deliver reliable power at the lowest reasonable cost. Because utilities must justify expenditures to public utility commissions, signing above-market contracts for unproven, first-of-a-kind technologies exposes them to regulatory disallowance if a project faces delays, cost overruns, or technical failure. Utilities are therefore structurally incentivized to wait until a technology has demonstrated commercial reliability and competitive pricing.

Large corporate buyers—particularly hyperscalers and major tech firms—face very different incentives. Rather than answering to ratepayer regulators, they can absorb higher initial costs and technology risk on their own balance sheets, treating early offtake agreements as strategic investments. Driven by ambitious 24/7 carbon-free energy targets and urgent power demand for data centers, these corporates are willing to pay a "green premium" to secure future firm clean power and help pull nascent technologies down the cost curve. By providing the bankable revenue needed to finance first commercial deployments, corporate buyers effectively de-risk emerging clean energy so utilities can adopt it later.

points.why: The response mentions utilities’ reliability mandate and the need for demonstrated commercial reliability, but explains the delay through regulatory cost risk without establishing that grid reliability requires a multi-year operating record.
The response links 24/7 targets to demand for firm clean power but does not explain how hourly matching exposes gaps left by intermittent renewables.
The response describes corporate buyers’ ability to absorb financial risk but omits the in-house technical expertise needed to evaluate unproven technologies.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Large corporate buyers often sign first because they can justify paying a premium for early clean power. A long-term offtake agreement can help them meet climate goals, secure power for growing operations, and lock in prices. Their creditworthiness can also give lenders enough confidence to finance a first commercial project.

Regulated utilities typically have to show that a contract is a prudent use of ratepayer money and that the project can reliably deliver the power they’re counting on. For an emerging technology, costs, construction timelines, and operating performance are harder to verify. The first corporate-backed projects give utilities and their regulators real-world evidence to evaluate later deals.

quotes: the project can reliably deliver the power they’re counting on
The first corporate-backed projects give utilities and their regulators real-world evidence to evaluate later deals.

points.why: The response mentions climate goals without explaining how hourly matching exposes gaps in wind and solar generation.
The response explains how corporate creditworthiness helps finance early projects but omits the in-house technical expertise needed to evaluate unproven technologies.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer: Large corporate buyers can justify paying a premium for early projects because round-the-clock clean power helps them meet climate goals, and backing a first project can secure future supply. They can take that risk with their own money. Regulated utilities, by contrast, usually have to show regulators that a long-term contract is prudent for the customers who will pay for it. That case is harder to make when a technology has little operating history and its costs and reliability are uncertain. A corporate offtake agreement gives the developer a revenue commitment it can use to raise financing. Once the project operates, utilities have evidence on cost and performance to support a contract of their own.

points.why: The response explains the need for operating evidence through regulatory prudence and leaves out utilities’ responsibility for keeping the grid reliable.
The response mentions round-the-clock clean power without explaining how hourly matching exposes gaps that intermittent renewables alone cannot fill.
The response describes corporate buyers’ ability to fund early projects without identifying the in-house technical expertise needed to evaluate unproven technologies.
